newsitem.title: ITALY: SOCCER-ITALY'S MAGNIFICENT SEVEN ARE DOWN TO FOUR.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-ITALY'S MAGNIFICENT SEVEN ARE DOWN TO FOUR.

text.p: At the start of the soccer season, there were seven foreign coaches walking tall in Italy's serie A and most wanted glory as well as gold.

Briton Roy Hodgson cracked the whip at free-spending Internazionale while Uruguayan Oscar Washington Tabarez arrived at league champions AC Milan hoping to emulate his European Cup-winning predecessors Fabio Capello and Arrigo Sacchi.
Roma welcomed balding Argentine Carlos Bianchi while rivals Lazio kept faith with stonefaced Czech Zdenek Zeman.
Both clubs boasted that they had the men that it took to win titles in the world's toughest league.
Sampdoria retained Sweden's trusty Sven-Goran Eriksson, a cool coach with years of local experience, while smaller sides Cagliari and Reggiana went for out-of-towners.
The Sardinians brought in Uruguayan hired hand Gregorio Perez while Reggiana went for Romanian Mircea Lucescu to help in the battle to stave off relegation to serie B.
With only a few months of the season completed, September's magnificent seven are suddenly left counting their losses as a fenced-in foursome while home-grown coaches have been calling the shots.
Perez was the first casualty.
He was run out of town in October, leaving Cagliari third from bottom with just four points.
In the first whiff of a fightback by the home nation's coaches, the Uruguayan was replaced by Carlo Mazzone -- the man who Roma pushed aside to make way for Bianchi.
Lucescu was next to bite the bullet.
The writing was probably on the wall from the day his appointment was announced when fans at an away game in Verona unfurled a banner reading "Lucescu? No Thank you."
"The fans don't know me so they can't judge me," he replied confidently. "I am convinced the players will help me."
Wrong. The Romanian failed to win any of his 10 league matches in charge and left last month.
In the most painful blow for the Romanian's pride, Reggiana then deemed that Francesco Oddo -- an Italian coach with no prior experience in serie A -- would do a better job.
On Monday, Tabarez completed the trio, replaced by Sacchi -- the third Italian to regain control of a top club.
AC Milan had appointed the cerebral Uruguayan to fill the gaping boots of Fabio Capello, the man who had led them to four league titles in five years and the European Cup.
The contrast proved too much, particularly as the Italian champions' form slumped dramatically.

When Tabarez packed his bags, after just 22 matches at the club, he left Milan out of the Italian Cup, ninth in the league and in severe danger of being dumped out of the cash-laden Champions' League following two defeats.

By contrast, Capello was reviving the fortunes of Real Madrid in Spain, taking them to the top of the league just as Giovanni Trapattoni, who walked out of Cagliari last season, enjoyed a run of form with German leaders Bayern Munich.

For many Italian soccer fans, it looks as if the country -- hit by an exodus of leading international players such as Fabrizio Ravanelli, Gianluca Vialli and Gianfranco Zola to England -- has exported quality and imported duds.
"Foreigner is not synonymous with incapable," insisted Tabarez this week, when comparisons were made.
"Capello and Trapattoni are two great coaches but not just because they coached in Italy. There are some who are not much good among the Italians as well," said Tabarez.
"Coaches are coaches, whether foreign or not...What's the point in comparing us with Trap and Capello."

Bologna coach Renzo Ulivieri, whose team is one of several low-budget provincial sides doing well at the moment, said there was a simple significance behind the fact that all three replaced coaches were foreigners.
"The Italian championship is very tough. There are a thousand ways of playing and that tactical uniformity you get elsewhere is lacking," he said.
"A coach who comes from abroad needs time to adapt, to understand. Eriksson, for example, had that time given to him and he, bit by bit, has become Italian."
Time was not something any of the clubs could offer, particularly when it meant money -- in European revenues for Milan or the lifeline of serie A for the others.
Eriksson, who has now spent five years at Sampdoria, is the only foreign coach sleeping soundly at the moment.
By contrast, Parma's Carlo Ancelotti is one Italian coach whose future may not be at his current club.

Hodgson has recently signed a new contract with Inter but was the object of much dismissal speculation earlier in the season and cannot rest easy at a club that expects success as a right in return for its huge outlay on players.
Bianchi and Zeman have also been give the dreaded backing of their club presidents, although the Argentine seems to be enjoying a respite from the early season pressure.
Zeman however remains odds-on favourite as the next foreigner to be ambushed. Lazio are out of the Italian cup, out of Europe and struggling in the league.
A fistful of league points is all he needs.
